variants.name: java.util.function.Predicate composition
variants.implementation_notes: Java ships the core of the pattern in the standard library: java.util.function.Predicate<T> is a functional interface whose default methods and(Predicate), or(Predicate) and negate() return composed predicates with short-circuit evaluation, so leaf rules are lambdas or method references and the And/Or/Not classes of the DDD texts disappear. Use Predicate for in-memory rules and for API-level composition; choose the Spring Data JPA Specification variant when the rule has to produce a WHERE clause, and the classic abstract-Specification hierarchy when rules must be named, introspected, serialized or logged - a lambda has no useful toString and cannot be translated.
pitfalls: and/or evaluate left to right with short-circuiting, so a predicate with side effects can be skipped silently; predicates must stay pure.
A lambda cannot be inspected: logging, serialization, translation to SQL and specific rejection messages all need a named class/record (or the JPA variant).
Predicate.negate/isEqual reject null arguments with NullPointerException; null candidates must be handled before or inside the rule.
Filtering a loaded collection in a Stream hides the fact that the rule belongs in the query - the classic full-scan/N+1 mistake.

variants.name: Spring Data JPA Specification over the Criteria API
variants.implementation_notes: The enterprise Java realization: a specification is an object whose toPredicate(Root<T>, CriteriaQuery<?>, CriteriaBuilder) returns a jakarta.persistence.criteria.Predicate. Spring Data composes them with and/or/not and the allOf/anyOf factories and executes them through JpaSpecificationExecutor, so the same rule drives repository queries. Choose it when the rule must run in SQL; keep the Criteria types and the persistence API out of the domain layer, or the domain depends on the store - exactly the trade-off the pattern's critics point at.
pitfalls: toPredicate may return null to mean no restriction; combining nulls can silently drop conditions, so composites must treat null as an identity element explicitly.
Navigating associations inside a specification creates joins you did not intend (N+1 or cartesian products); fetch joins and entity graphs must be planned alongside the rule.
Putting Root/CriteriaBuilder in domain classes couples the model to JPA and makes the rule untestable without the provider; keep the translator at the persistence boundary.
jakarta.persistence replaced javax.persistence: a spec written against the old namespace fails on modern stacks.

variants.name: Hand-written abstract Specification with And/Or/Not subclasses
variants.implementation_notes: The layout from the DDD literature: an abstract Specification<T> declaring isSatisfiedBy(T), one subclass per rule with the varying values as constructor parameters, and generic AndSpecification/OrSpecification/NotSpecification composites holding children in a collection. Choose it when rules are instantiated from configuration, need stable class names in logs/metrics, or must be combined dynamically on a pre-Java-8 toolchain; on Java 8+ the same behaviour is less code with Predicate, so keep the hierarchy only where its inspectability is actually used.
pitfalls: One class per criterion plus generic combinators is a lot of ceremony for rules that a Predicate composes in one line; the hierarchy earns its keep only through naming, logging or dynamic construction.
Hand-written composites must replicate short-circuiting and null handling that the library variants provide; untested combinators are a common source of subtle differences.
Holding children in a mutable collection lets callers mutate a composite after it has been shared.
